newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's Cardoso ponders seeking re-election.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's Cardoso ponders seeking re-election.

text.p: President Fernando Henrique Cardoso said in an interview being published on Sunday he was considering running for a second term, confirming that he wanted to become Brazil's first president to be re-elected.
Asked if he would run in the 1998 elections if the constitution was revised to allow the possibility and the economic stability he introduced stayed on track, he replied, "I would."

"I am in favour of re-election as an idea, and if the constitution were to be rewritten, I think I should have the right to stand," the president told veteran political reporter Elio Gaspari in the interview, conducted for the newspapers O Globo and O Estado de Sao Paulo.

Until now, Cardoso has limited himself to discreet comments in favour of the theory of re-election, declining to say whether he wanted to emulate his Peruvian and Argentine counterparts, both of whom rewrote their respective constitutions to allow them to stand for, and win, second terms.

In Sunday's interview, Cardoso continued to shy away from explicitly saying he would be a candidate in 1998. "A president can't say he wants this or that. You have to feel whether or not society is willing to accept it," he was quoted as saying.

So far Brazilian society seems less than enthusiastic about re-election, which for many still smacks of the authoritarianism of the country's rule by imperial Portugal and of the 1964-85 military dictatorship. A recent poll found 62 percent of those questioned were against the idea of Cardoso's running again.
Another poll showed support of just 40 percent of members of Congress, where the re-election debate is expected to begin in October with the first meeting of a lower house committee.

Observers say the president faces the toughest test of his two years in power in trying to get a constitutional amendment allowing re-election through a volatile Chamber of Deputies, where his ambitions will clash with those of other would-be presidents.

Cardoso himself, in an interview published on the eve of election day in 1994, said re-election would prove too hot an issue to touch during his term. "Imagine what a campaign for re-electing a sitting president would be like. He is liable to lose everything, because everyone will say he is using the state machine to get what he wants," Cardoso was quoted as saying.

On the president's side in the re-election debate are the country's powerful state governors and mayors, who are also currently banned from re-election but would be granted the chance of a second term by the proposed legislative changes.

In Sunday's interview, the president considered the possibility of the amendment's being defeated in Congress but said any successor would be bound to continue his policies of fiscal restraint, which have slashed Brazil's once sky-high inflation and kept Cardoso's personal approval ratings high.

"Like it or not, Brazil is on a clear path," he told the newspapers. "Now we are facing the possibilty of ending next year with single-digit inflation. You want to know something? I never thought I would see that day."
